pll1d27c3-d1e3501.summary: States that each property belongs properly to one person, and by them the persons are determined and differ but do not separate.
claims: The properties determine and distinguish the persons.
The persons do not separate from one another.

pll1d27c3-d1e3504.summary: Cites John Damascene: hypostases do not differ in substance but in characteristic, determining properties, which belong to hypostases, not nature.
claims: Hypostases differ by characteristic properties, not substance.

pll1d27c3-d1e3519.summary: Further Damascene: the divine hypostasis of the Word is timeless and eternal, simple, having all the Father has as consubstantial, differing from the Father's hypostasis by mode of birth and relation, never separating from it.
claims: The Word has all the Father has.
The Word differs from the Father by mode of birth, not by separation.

pll1d27c3-d1e3532.summary: Further Damascene: we recognize the difference of persons in the paternal, filial, and processional properties, but the hypostases are inseparable, united without confusion and divided without distance. Each is perfect and has its own mode of existence, but they are united in substance and do not separate from the Father's hypostasis.
claims: The persons differ by paternal, filial, and processional properties.
They are united without confusion and divided without distance.

pll1d27c3-d1e3544.summary: Notes that here the three properties signified variously above are distinguished.
claims: The three properties are paternity, filiation, and procession.

pll1d27c3-d1e3547.summary: Adds that besides Father, Son, and Holy Spirit there are other names that signify the persons and denote the same properties and are relative: begetter, begotten, Word, Image.
claims: Begetter, begotten, Word, and Image are personal, relative names.

pll1d27c3-d1e3552.summary: Cites De Trinitate V: 'begotten' signifies what 'son' does, and as son refers to father, so begotten to begetter.
claims: 'Begotten' signifies the same as 'Son.'

pll1d27c3-d1e3581.summary: Cites De Trinitate VI: only the Son is called Word, not Father and Son together; similarly only the Son is the Image of the Father.
claims: Only the Son is the Word.
Only the Son is the Image.

pll1d27c3-d1e3596.summary: Cites De Trinitate VII: as wisdom and essence the Word is what the Father is; as Word he is not, since the Word is not the Father and is said relatively like Son.
claims: As Word, the Son is said relatively.
As wisdom and essence, he is what the Father is.

pll1d27c3-d1e3615.summary: Further Augustine: as son refers to father, so word refers to the one whose word it is, so he is not called Word by what he is called wisdom. He is Word as he is Son; he is wisdom as essence, and Father and Son are one essence and wisdom.
claims: The Son is Word by the same relation by which he is Son.
The Son is wisdom by essence.

pll1d27c3-d1e3636.summary: Further Augustine: the Father is not the Word, nor Son, nor Image; it would be absurd for an image to be said 'ad se.'
claims: The Father is not Word or Image.
An image is necessarily relative.

pll1d27c3-d1e3648.summary: Cites De Trinitate V: Son, Word, and Image are said relatively, all referring to the Father, and none is said of the Father.
claims: Son, Word, and Image are relative to the Father.

pll1d27c3-d1e3663.summary: Concludes that Word and Image, like Son or begotten, are said relatively to the Father, by the same property or notion as Son; but he is not called wisdom or essence by the notion by which he is Word, since wisdom is said by essence, not relation.
claims: Word and Image are said by the same notion as Son.
Wisdom is said by essence, not relation.

pl-l1d27c3.summary: Holds that the properties belong to single persons and determine and distinguish them without separating them. John Damascene: hypostases differ by characteristic properties, not substance; the Word is consubstantial with the Father, differing by mode of birth but never separating; the persons differ in paternal, filial, and processional properties, and are united without confusion and distinguished without distance. Other personal names, begetter, begotten, Word, Image, also signify persons and their properties and are relative. With Augustine, 'begotten' means the same as 'Son'; only the Son is Word and Image; 'Word' is relative like 'Son,' while 'wisdom' is said by essence.
claims: Personal properties determine and distinguish the persons without separating them.
Hypostases differ by characteristic properties, not substance.
The persons are united without confusion and distinct without distance.
Begetter, begotten, Word, and Image are personal, relative names.
'Begotten' signifies the same as 'Son.'
Only the Son is Word and Image.
The Son is called Word and Image by the same property by which he is Son; he is called wisdom by essence.
